_comment: The health contract: ONE answer key, four frameworks.
Feature 8. Health is consumed by something EXTERNAL - a Kubernetes httpGet
probe, a load balancer, an uptime monitor - so the path, the JSON key set
and the status code ARE the feature. Everything below was decided in
ADR-0016 and is covered by a real, no-mock test in the named suite.
Kubernetes reads the STATUS CODE and never the body: HTTPGetAction has no
body-matching field, and success is 200 <= code < 400. That is why the key
set is small and why a failure must be non-2xx rather than a flag in JSON.
scripts/audit-health-contract.py checks that every named suite exists and
carries every named case, so this file cannot rot into a wish.

body.note: EXACTLY these four, in all four frameworks. No extras.

invariants.rule: The health endpoint is a LIVENESS probe. It answers 200 whenever the process can answer at all. A recorded route error never changes the status code, and stale .broken sentinels from a previous run are cleared at boot.
invariants.why: A liveness failure tells Kubernetes to RESTART the container, so it may only react to conditions a restart repairs. A route that raised wrote a .broken sentinel from the request path; Python returned 503 while one existed and nothing cleared them, so ONE bad request took the endpoint down permanently and across restarts. Rails states the same reasoning for probing nothing: an app reporting down because a dependency is down 'may be restarted unnecessarily'.
invariants.applies_to_note: php, ruby and node never had a failure path, so there was nothing to remove; the rule binds them if one is ever added.
cases: health is 200 before any route error
a route error does not flip health to 503
stale broken files are cleared at boot

invariants.rule: The body carries exactly status, version, uptime and framework. uptime is seconds as a float. Nothing else is added.
invariants.why: It is a wire contract whose whole point is being identical in four frameworks, and Kubernetes never reads it, so every extra key is weight on a probe path for no consumer. Python carried errors/latest_error; once those stopped driving the status code they were diagnostics, and diagnostics belong on the dev dashboard, which still reads .broken.
cases: the body is exactly the four contract keys

invariants.rule: The configured path (TINA4_HEALTH_PATH, default /__health) is registered, AND /health is registered as well, always. Setting the env var adds a path and never removes one.
invariants.why: PHP defaulted to /health and registered the configured path ONLY, so /__health 404ed on a default install and setting the env var silently deleted the path an existing load balancer was already using. Either one takes a pod out of rotation on upgrade.
cases: the legacy slash health path serves 200
a custom health path from the environment serves 200
the legacy slash health path survives a custom health path

invariants.rule: Registering the health routes is unconditional. It is idempotent because Router.add replaces a repeated (method, path) in place, not because anything asks the router whether health is already there.
invariants.why: Ruby guarded with find_route('/health', 'GET') while the signature is find_route(METHOD, PATH). The swapped arguments usually matched nothing, but an ANY route matches any path, so an ordinary catch-all made the guard fire and health was never registered: a probe received the application's catch-all response instead. Asking the router 'does something answer here' can never distinguish 'health is registered' from 'something else matches'.
cases: registers both the configured path and the legacy /health
still registers health when the app has a catch-all ANY route
does not duplicate routes when called more than once
re-registers after Router.clear! wipes the table

invariants.rule: Python emits `uptime` (float seconds) and `framework` "tina4-python", matching its three siblings and the published docs.
invariants.why: Python was the outlier on both, against the other three frameworks AND against its own documentation, which already said `uptime`. No standard prescribes `uptime_seconds`; the one convention covering JSON health bodies (draft-inadarei-api-health-check-06 s4.4) keeps the key bare and puts the unit in a sibling field.
cases: uptime is reported as seconds under the uptime key
the framework is named tina4 python

specified_not_built.rule: A readiness endpoint, separate from liveness, probes the dependencies an app has actually configured and returns 503 when one is down. Readiness withdraws traffic and never restarts.
specified_not_built.why: Liveness restarts; readiness withdraws. A dependency check on liveness turns one database outage into a fleet-wide restart loop that cannot fix the database. No framework probes any dependency today, so this is a new feature rather than a fix.

specified_not_built.rule: Every Dockerfile, repo and generated, carries a HEALTHCHECK pointing at the liveness path.
specified_not_built.why: Not one of the four repo Dockerfiles, and none of the generated ones, has a HEALTHCHECK today. Whoever adds it must BUILD each image and watch the container reach healthy: several images are Alpine or distroless, and a HEALTHCHECK calling curl in an image without curl fails every probe. Note for the docs: plain `docker run` does not restart a container on healthcheck failure; only Swarm and Kubernetes act on it.
specified_not_built.status: not built - could not be verified on the audit machine (no Docker daemon)
